I need to review how organizations are listed, how activity is recorded, and invoice number uniqueness. I also need to check notification schema constraints and existing tests for jobs and billing.

I will also examine notification kinds, activity actions, webhook schemas, invoice emails, migrations, and job manifests. Period math needs careful review: a period spans from its start up to its end.

Periods end on the same day and time of the next month or year, clamping to the last valid day when necessary. Each new period starts exactly where the previous one ends. A clamped day carries forward; for example, January 31 becomes February 28, and that date becomes March 28.

In a leap year, January 31 carries forward to February 29. The next period would then start on March 29.

The day used for clamping is the current period start, not an original anchor. Annual periods follow the same rule: 29 February clamps to 28 February and carries forward. The time of day must be preserved exactly, including hours, minutes, seconds, and milliseconds. The implementation will use UTC.

The `addPeriod` function extracts UTC components from the start date. For annual intervals, it adds one year and clamps the day to the target month's last valid day.

Monthly periods add one month and carry the clamped day forward. The `daysInMonth` helper will compute a month's length from its zero-indexed year and month.

Edge cases for month-end dates are confirmed: March 31 becomes April 30, and December 31 becomes January 31. The codebase uses ISO timestamps via `toIsoTimestamp`. Proration logic for "days left" still needs review.

Days left are calculated as the ceiling of the remaining duration in days, rounded up to whole days. A started day counts as a full day even if only part of it remains. The count becomes zero once the period end has been reached.

Period length is the rounded number of days between its start and end, with a minimum of one. UTC month-end clamping produces exact whole-day counts.

Proration scales the full-period amount by the ratio of days left to total period days, then rounds down to whole cents. A zero charge produces no invoice. The prorated invoice covers the current period.

The full-period charge equals the plan's monthly price per seat multiplied by the subscription's seats and the number of months in the period. Seat additions are prorated against that same amount. Removing seats or changing seats on a free plan or during a trial incurs no charge. These adjustments only apply to paid, active subscriptions.

The seat-addition proration formula is now defined: multiply the plan price per seat by the number of seats added and the months in the period, then scale by days left over total period days and round down to whole cents. A charge is only issued if the result is greater than zero.

Past-due and canceled subscriptions are excluded from this rule. Only active subscriptions qualify for seat changes.

Plan changes between paid plans on an active subscription are prorated. The charge equals the price difference per seat multiplied by seats and months in the period, rounded down to whole cents. Downgrades and unchanged plans incur no charge, and the period remains unchanged. Choosing a plan during a trial costs nothing and preserves the trial period.

Leaving the free plan for a paid one starts a fresh period at that moment with the chosen interval, invoiced in full. Moving to the free plan charges nothing.

The existing `updateSubscriptionPlan` logic forces the subscription status to "active" and does not alter the period. The new requirement for trial plan changes conflicts with this: it mandates keeping the trial period and deferring the first invoice until the trial ends, which would mean preserving the "trialing" status rather than switching to "active".

The existing code forces the subscription to active status and does not alter the trial period dates. The requirement instead calls for keeping the trial period intact, which means preserving the current period boundaries and deferring the first invoice until that period ends.

The existing function will keep updating the billing interval. Only leaving the free plan for a paid one will skip the period reset. Changing the interval while staying on the same paid plan counts as an unchanged plan, so no charge applies and the period remains unchanged.
